text:
Based on the provided evidence, American cities underwent a fundamental transformation between 1980 and 2024 characterized by accelerating gentrification, rising inequality, declining affordability relative to income growth, and significant demographic shifts. [Source: ev-1]

### **Gentrification Trends (1980–2020)**
American cities have experienced dramatic economic and demographic changes since 1980 [Source: ev-1]. Gentrification accelerated significantly after 2000, with rates doubling compared to the 1990s; specifically, nearly 20% of lower-income neighborhoods in major cities experienced gentrification since 2000 Census data was collected, compared to only 9% during the 1990 period. [Source: ev-1] By the period from 2000 to 2020, income-based gentrification became the dominant form, having been rare in the 1970s and 1980s. [Source: ev-1]

The intensity of this transformation varied by city. The most intensive gentrification occurred in Portland (58.1% of eligible tracts), Washington D.C. (51.9%), Minneapolis (50.6%), and Seattle (50%). [Source: ev-1] Regional patterns show that Pacific Northwest cities, Northeast Corridor metros like Boston, New York, and Washington D.C., and select Sun Belt cities such as Atlanta exhibited these intensive transformation patterns most frequently. [Source: ev-1] In terms of raw totals, the highest number of tracts (128) gentrified in New York. [Source: ev-1]

In gentrifying neighborhoods, populations increased by an average of 6.5%, poverty rates decreased by 0.7 percentage points, and areas became whiter with a 4.3 percentage point increase in non-Hispanic white residents. [Source: ev-1] Conversely, non-gentrifying low-income areas saw population losses (-2.4%) and an increase in poverty of 6.7 percentage points. [Source: ev-1] Displacement patterns show that residents from historically Black gentrifying neighborhoods tend to move to poorer non-gentrifying areas, while residents from other gentrifying neighborhoods move to wealthier ones, indicating that minority communities face more challenges during this process. [Source: ev-1]

### **Rising Inequality (2007–2024)**
Inequality has widened steadily over the last four decades. The U.S. Gini coefficient reached 0.40 by 2013, but major metropolitan areas experienced much steeper increases; for instance, New York City’s Gini coefficient was 0.5469 compared to the national average of 0.40 in 2013. [Source: ev-1] Atlanta and Miami recorded coefficients of 0.57, while New Orleans reached 0.56. [Source: ev-1] Several metros displayed extreme inequality patterns with Gini coefficients exceeding 0.54 and income ratios reaching 18:1 between top and bottom earners. [Source: ev-1]

Specific income ratio analyses highlight this disparity. The 80/20 income ratio analysis shows New Orleans at 7.87 (the 80th percentile earns nearly 8 times more than the 20th) and Boston at 7.81, where the 80th percentile earned $172,476 versus just $22,095 for the 20th percentile in that city's data set. [Source: ev-1] Furthermore, the 95/20 ratio reached 18:1 in Atlanta and Washington D.C., meaning the 95th percentile earns 18 times more than the bottom quintile. [Source: ev-1]

Historical trends confirm this widening gap; research documents that 57 of the 100 largest metropolitan areas had significantly higher inequality in 2014 compared to 2007. [Source: ev-1] The financial crisis accelerated these dynamics, with the national 95/20 rising from a baseline context where Bridgeport, New Orleans, San Francisco, Boston, and New Haven were most affected between 2007 and 2014. [Source: ev-1] In San Francisco specifically, top incomes rose by approximately $120,000 between 2014 and 2016. [Source: ev-1] Federal Reserve data tracking over 3,140 inequality series confirms that inequality reached record levels by 2018–2021, marking the sharpest increase among advanced economies since the 1980s. [Source: ev-1]

### **Affordability and Economic Mobility (2000–2024)**
While urban areas have seen substantial nominal income growth, affordability has deteriorated relative to housing costs. Since 2000, home prices increased by 177%, while median household income grew only 92%. [Source: ev-1] The Case-Shiller Index reached 325.78 in July 2024, representing a 225% increase since January 2000. [Source: ev-1] Price-to-income ratios illustrate this strain; California cities show ratios between 9.6 and 12.2, more than double the national average of 4.7. [Source: ev-1]

Economic mobility for low-income families has also declined. Data confirms that 48 of the 50 largest metros experienced worsening economic mobility over a 15-year period (comparing outcomes for those growing up in the 1990s versus the 1980). Only Houston showed improvement, gaining a 1.1% increase in income outcomes. [Source: ev-1] This decline coincides with structural shifts where manufacturing jobs fell from 19.5 million in 1979 to under 11.5 million during the pandemic, while finance and professional services grew from 12 million to 32 million jobs, concentrating high-income professionals in urban cores. [Source: ev-1]

### **Demographic Shifts and Displacement (1980–Present)**
Urban demographics have changed significantly since 1980. Nearly 80% of the country's under-45 population growth was concentrated in metro areas over 1 million residents. Urban counties gained prime-age workers (ages 25–54), whereas rural counties lost this demographic. [Source: ev-1] The educational profile of cities has shifted as well; urban areas now have 35% of residents with bachelor’s degrees or higher, compared to 31% in suburbs and 19% in rural areas. [Source: ev-1]

Racial composition changes are evident but complex. Since 2000, the white population share fell by 7 points in urban cores and 8 points in suburbs. Currently, 53% of urban counties are majority nonwhite, compared to only 10% of suburban counties. However, gentrifying neighborhoods themselves became whiter during their transformation. [Source: ev-1]
